identification.summary: Storm-0940 is Microsoft's name for a Chinese threat actor that Microsoft says has been active since at least 2021 and obtains initial access through password spray and brute-force attacks, or by exploiting or misusing network edge applications and services [S1]. Microsoft observed it using credentials harvested by CovertNetwork-1658, a covert network of compromised small-office/home-office routers, sometimes on the same day the credentials were obtained [S1]. After access it uses scanning and credential-dumping tools for lateral movement, tries to reach network devices, installs proxy tools and remote access trojans for persistence, and attempts data exfiltration [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: active since at least 2021 [S1]. Microsoft began observing intrusions enabled by CovertNetwork-1658 password spraying in August 2023 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft tracks Storm-0940 (the actor) separately from CovertNetwork-1658 (the router network), which is also called xlogin and Quad7 (7777) [S1]. Microsoft assesses that multiple Chinese threat actors use credentials from CovertNetwork-1658, so the network is not exclusive to Storm-0940 [S1]. Public research on the botnet itself (Gi7w0rm, Sekoia, Team Cymru) predates Microsoft's actor naming; those vendors did not name Storm-0940 in the coverage reviewed [S3][S4].

attribution.confidence: Microsoft calls the actor Chinese and assesses that the CovertNetwork-1658 operator is located in China [S1]. Microsoft describes the hand-off of credentials between the network and Storm-0940 as evidence of a likely close working relationship [S1].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry on sign-in activity and on the same-day reuse of sprayed credentials [S1]. No government attribution or named sponsoring agency was found in the sources reviewed.

targeting.notes: Microsoft lists these sectors as 'among others' [S1]. Sekoia described the botnet as mainly used for brute-force attempts against Microsoft 365 accounts [S3]. Gi7w0rm earlier described low-volume brute-forcing of Microsoft Azure instances (October 2023) [S4]. Microsoft saw an increase in targeted Azure tenants between 8 and 30 October 2024 [S1].

capabilities.summary: Initial access through low-volume password spraying relayed via compromised SOHO routers (mostly TP-Link), plus brute force and exploitation or misuse of network edge applications [S1]. Microsoft says the spray submits very few attempts across many accounts, and in about 80 percent of cases only one sign-in attempt per account per day, so per-IP or per-account failure thresholds will not catch it [S1]. The router network was historically about 8,000 devices, about 20 percent spraying at once, average node uptime about 90 days [S1]. Routers are compromised through a remote-code-execution vulnerability that Microsoft says it is still investigating; the implant chain downloads a Telnet binary and the xlogin backdoor from a remote FTP server, opens a command shell on TCP 7777, then deploys a SOCKS5 server on TCP 11288 [S1]. Sekoia later reported operators developing new backdoors and reverse shells, and additional clusters on other devices (alogin on ASUS, rlogin on Ruckus, axlogin on Axentra NAS, zylogin on Zyxel VPNs) [S3]. After access, Storm-0940 uses scanning and credential-dumping tools, proxy tools and RATs; specific tool names are not given in the Microsoft post [S1].

campaigns.name: Quad7 (7777) botnet first publicly documented
campaigns.summary: Independent researcher Gi7w0rm first referenced the 7777 botnet, estimated at about 10,000 nodes and used for low-volume brute-forcing of Microsoft Azure instances. This is research on the botnet, not yet linked to Storm-0940 by name [S4].

campaigns.name: Password-spray-enabled intrusions begin
campaigns.summary: Microsoft begins observing intrusions enabled by CovertNetwork-1658 password spraying against its customers [S1].

campaigns.name: Team Cymru report on botnet 7777
campaigns.summary: Team Cymru counted 12,783 active bots over the 30 days to 5 August 2024 across the 7777 and a second 63256 (mostly ASUS) cluster, with seven management IPs [S4].

campaigns.name: Sekoia documents xlogin and sibling clusters
campaigns.summary: Sekoia describes xlogin (TP-Link, ports 7777 and 11288) and four sibling clusters, mainly used against Microsoft 365 accounts, and notes a decline in the xlogin botnet [S3].

campaigns.name: Microsoft names Storm-0940 and CovertNetwork-1658
campaigns.summary: On 31 October 2024 Microsoft publishes its assessment linking Storm-0940 to CovertNetwork-1658 credentials, notes network usage declined after the July and August 2024 vendor reports, and a rise in targeted Azure tenants from 8 to 30 October, which it says may be early evidence of new infrastructure with modified fingerprints [S1].

diamond.adversary: Chinese actor tracked by Microsoft as Storm-0940, in a likely close working relationship with the China-based CovertNetwork-1658 operator [S1].
diamond.capability: Low-volume password spray, brute force, edge-application exploitation, credential dumping, proxy tools and RATs [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: CovertNetwork-1658 / Quad7: compromised SOHO routers (mostly TP-Link) with xlogin shell on TCP 7777 and SOCKS5 on TCP 11288, about 8,000 devices, FTP-hosted implant downloads [S1]. Microsoft lists two spoofed user-agent strings and an Azure app ID in hunting guidance; it published no IPs, hashes or domains [S1].
diamond.victim: Think tanks, government, NGOs, law firms, defense industrial base in North America and Europe [S1].
diamond.technology: Cloud identity (Microsoft Entra/Azure AD, Microsoft 365) accounts lacking MFA or relying on legacy authentication, and unmanaged consumer routers used as proxies [S1][S3].

gaps: Sponsoring organization and strategic objectives are not stated in the sources reviewed; the encyclopedia country field (CN) comes from Microsoft's description.
The router vulnerability used to build CovertNetwork-1658 is unidentified; Microsoft said it was still investigating [S1].
Names of the post-compromise tools (credential dumpers, proxies, RATs) are not given in the Microsoft post [S1].
Which other Chinese actors use the same credentials is not public [S1].
No Storm-0940 reporting after November 2024 was found; current activity and whether new infrastructure materialized are unknown.
Sekoia's and Gi7w0rm's primary reports and Microsoft's naming page were not opened directly; Sekoia and Team Cymru details come from press and vendor coverage [S3][S4].
Source disagreement on the SOCKS5 port (11288 versus 11228) appears in press coverage; Microsoft states 11288 [S1][S3].
Overlap with other Microsoft or vendor actor names (for example any MITRE group) is unverified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Cloud identity tenants (Microsoft 365/Entra) used by DoD-adjacent contractors, think tanks and law firms are key terrain, as is any internet-facing edge application [S1]. STEP 2: The adversary hides spray traffic in residential and small-office router IPs, so source-IP reputation and per-account lockouts are weak defenses [S1]. STEP 3: The template is router-proxied low-and-slow spray, then same-day valid-credential logon, then scanning, credential dumping, proxy/RAT persistence and exfiltration attempts [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued spraying against government, defense industrial base and policy organizations in North America and Europe, using refreshed router infrastructure [S1]. MDCOA is use of the same shared credential pool by several Chinese actors against a single DIB tenant during a crisis; Microsoft says multiple actors use these credentials [S1]. Candidate indicators: sign-ins using the user-agent strings and app ID in Microsoft's hunting guidance, one-attempt-per-account failures spread across many accounts and source ISPs, logons from consumer ISP addresses inconsistent with user geography [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: feed identity-provider sign-in telemetry, including failed-attempt patterns across many accounts, into the common operational picture; single-IP thresholds will miss this activity [S1]. (2) Authorities: blocking or lockout actions on contractor tenants rest with the tenant owner; coordinate through DC3 and DIB cybersecurity channels rather than assuming DoD authority. (3) Mission assurance: enforce MFA with no exclusions, disable legacy authentication and move to phishing-resistant methods, as Microsoft recommends, for mission-critical accounts [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with Microsoft and partners; because multiple actors reuse the credentials, prioritize containment and password resets over attribution [S1].

provenance.importedSummary: Storm-0940 is a Chinese threat actor active since at least 2021, known for gaining initial access through password spray and brute-force attacks, as well as exploiting network edge applications. Microsoft has observed Storm-0940 utilizing valid credentials obtained from CovertNetwork-1658's password spray operations, indicating a close operational relationship between the two. Once inside a victim environment, Storm-0940 has been seen leveraging compromised credentials for further malicious activities. Additionally, Storm-0940 has employed botnets, such as Quad7, to facilitate password spraying attacks.
